rows.verified: Electromagnetic fields are produced whenever electrical or electronic equipment is used.
Workplace EMFs include static electric, static magnetic and time-varying electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields up to 300 GHz.
Regulated sensory effects include nausea, vertigo and flickering sensations in peripheral vision.
Regulated health effects include shocks, nerve stimulation and heating effects.
Indirect EMF risks include interference with implanted or body-worn medical devices and attraction of ferromagnetic objects in strong static fields.
Employers must assess the EMF levels to which employees may be exposed.
Employers must ensure exposure remains below applicable exposure-limit values and take action when limits are exceeded.
Workers likely to be exposed require information and training based on the EMF risk assessment.
EMF risk depends on frequency, field strength, distance, exposure duration, work activity, shielding and the presence of implanted or body-worn medical devices.
EMF evidence is source-, task-, exposure- and person-specific and is not an exact parcel-level sensory or health-effect probability.
The decision to use a pesticide should form part of a thorough risk assessment and an integrated pest, weed or disease-management approach.
The pesticide definition includes plant-protection products and biocides.
The placing on the market, storage, use and disposal of pesticides are subject to regulatory controls.
Users must read and understand the product label, safety-data sheet and supplied instructions before use.
Reasonable precautions are required to protect human health and the environment during pesticide storage, use and disposal.
Pesticides should not be carried in a vehicle cab and should be kept in a secure leak-proof container or external locked cabinet separated from occupants.
People applying pesticides at work must be trained and competent for the task and use the protective measures specified by the product and assessment.
Businesses whose work involves plant-protection products may need to register under the Official Controls (Plant Protection Products) Regulations 2020.
Pesticide risk depends on the authorised product, concentration, application rate, exposure route, equipment, weather, spray drift, storage, PPE and environmental receptors.
Pesticide evidence is product-, application-, exposure- and environment-specific and is not an exact parcel-level poisoning or ecological-harm probability.
